screens.title: Capstone Project Kickoff & Design Document
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome to the capstone kickoff. This project is your chance to integrate Unity, C#, and design skills into a single, polished game you can show to employers or peers. The aim is not to build a blockbuster but to produce a complete, well-scoped playable experience that demonstrates your strengths. In this lesson you will learn why planning matters, how a Game Design Document acts as a single source of truth, and how to protect your schedule by defining a minimal viable product. I'll guide you through each GDD section — concept, core gameplay, art and audio, technical specs — and show practical ways to keep scope under control. You'll also get simple risk-management practices such as version control and realistic milestone planning. By the end you'll know what to write in your first GDD draft and how to use it every week to steer development. Think of this kickoff as building the map before you walk the terrain: the map doesn't limit creativity, it helps you finish. What is one small but essential feature your capstone must include?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Capstone Kickoff
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Capstone Project Kickoff & Design Document

Plan a manageable, demonstrable game using a living design document. Learn how to define scope and protect progress.

In this lesson
  • Why a capstone matters and what success looks like.
  • How to write a Game Design Document that guides development.
  • Techniques to avoid scope creep and protect your timeline.
Coming up

A step-by-step GDD outline, MVP planning, risk checkpoints, and a hands-on template you can copy into your notes.

Explore Key Topics
Start with a focused MVP, document the design, and protect progress with version control and risk planning.
Game Idea
Elevator pitch, genre, target audience. The seed of your capstone.
Core Loop
Player actions that repeat: input, challenge, reward.
MVP
A small set of must-have features that make the game playable and testable.
Quick note
Your GDD is living: update it after playtests and when you choose or reject stretch goals. Major changes should be recorded with reasons and new estimates.

screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the purpose of a capstone project, start a game with a clear vision, and write the first draft of a Game Design Document. You will learn to identify the GDD sections that matter most: high-level overview, core gameplay, art and audio direction, technical specifications, and a risk plan. You will also practice defining a minimal viable product, which protects your schedule and ensures a playable deliverable. Each objective includes a practical reason: employers and collaborators want demonstrable results, and a structured plan helps you prioritize work and make defensible trade-offs. We'll show examples of concrete MVP features and common vague statements to avoid. Finally, you'll be introduced to simple project-safety practices such as version control, realistic milestones, and short feedback loops to reduce burnout. These skills let you go from idea to a finished, playable capstone with confidence. Which objective do you want to start with first?

Learning Objectives

Understand planning, scope management, and a GDD-driven workflow for your capstone.

01. Purpose & Scope

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Outcomes & Habits

How these skills will help you

Translate design into durable, testable work and protect progress from common failures.

Weekly milestones
Break the MVP into 1-week goals to keep momentum and create playable checkpoints for feedback.
Daily commits
Commit early and often so experiments are reversible and progress is visible.
Risk log
Record high-risk items and backup plans to reduce surprises and protect your timeline.
Tip
Make your GDD specific: replace vague phrases like "fun combat" with measurable behaviors such as damage values, enemy patterns, and clear player feedback.

screens.title: What is a Capstone Project?
screens.narratorSegment: A capstone project is a culminating piece of work that gathers your skills into a single, demonstrable product. In game development, it's an opportunity to show you can design, implement, and polish a playable experience in Unity using C#. It matters because hiring teams and reviewers look for finished artifacts that reveal both creative design choices and technical competence. A common misconception is that bigger equals better. In reality, a focused, complete game that demonstrates thoughtful systems and polish beats an incomplete, sprawling concept. For example, a tight 2D platformer with a solid core loop, responsive controls, and a handful of levels will communicate more than an unfinished ambitious RPG. When planning, state your goals: is the capstone about showcasing gameplay, technical systems, or art direction? Choose one primary focus. Your takeaway is this: pick a realistic scope that highlights your strengths and commit to finishing the playable MVP. Which single skill do you want this capstone to showcase? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What is a Capstone?
What is a Capstone Project?

A culminating, demonstrable project that brings together design and technical skills into a single playable experience.

Definition
An integrative project showing practical mastery of Unity, C#, and design principles through a finished game.
Example
A polished 2D platformer with responsive controls, 6 levels, simple enemy AI, and clear win/lose states that you can play from start to finish.
Common mistake
Equating ambition with success. Adding too many features leads to incomplete projects and loss of polish.
Key Takeaway

Choose a focused goal for the capstone. Finish a small, well-crafted MVP rather than chase many features.

How to pick your capstone focus
  • Inventory your strengths: programming, level design, art, audio.
  • Pick one primary skill to highlight and two secondary goals at most.
  • Write a one-sentence elevator pitch to keep decisions aligned.
Closing question
Which single skill should your capstone make unmistakably clear to a reviewer?

screens.title: Why a Game Design Document (GDD)?
screens.narratorSegment: The Game Design Document is your project's compass. It collects the elevator pitch, target audience, mechanics, art and audio directions, and technical notes into one place so design decisions remain consistent over time. A common error is to treat the GDD as a static checklist. Instead, view it as living: update it after playtests, record why features changed, and use it to communicate with collaborators or future-you. Practically, start the GDD with a one-paragraph overview and a clear MVP list. Then expand the core gameplay section with concrete numbers: movement speeds, jump heights, enemy behavior patterns, and win/loss conditions. Being specific eliminates ambiguous goals like "fun combat." For example, note that an enemy patrols between two points, deals two damage per hit, and has a 0.5-second stagger when hit. That detail guides programming and tuning. The takeaway: a GDD reduces wasted effort and helps you finish by making decisions explicit. What would you write in your GDD's one-sentence elevator pitch? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › GDD Essentials
Why a Game Design Document?

It keeps your vision explicit, documents trade-offs, and serves as the single source of truth during development.

Process: How to use the GDD
  1. Write a one-paragraph overview and elevator pitch.
  2. List the MVP features and acceptance criteria for each.
  3. Record specific mechanics with numbers and examples.
  4. Update the document after playtests and major decisions.
Example
Instead of "fun combat," document: "Melee attack: 20 frames, 15 damage, 0.5s cooldown; enemy patrol behavior: point A to B, detects player within 3 units."
GDD Core Sections
  • Overview: Title, genre, target audience, elevator pitch.
  • Core Gameplay: mechanics, core loop, win/lose conditions.
  • World & Narrative: characters and mood.
  • Art & Audio: style, palette, UI direction.
  • Technical Specs: engine, language, platforms, tools.
Key Takeaway

Write specifics, not adjectives. The GDD is a tool to reduce ambiguity and speed iteration.

screens.title: GDD — High-level Overview & Elevator Pitch
screens.narratorSegment: Begin your GDD with a high-level overview that answers the core questions: what is the game, who is it for, and what makes it compelling? This includes a working title, genre, target audience, and a one- or two-sentence elevator pitch. Why is this important? Because a clear overview aligns every later decision with the game's primary goals. A vague pitch invites scope drift. For example, compare "a platformer with good combat" to "a bite-sized platformer where the player uses a charge-jump to navigate moving platforms and collect time shards across six short levels." The second version immediately suggests level design constraints and mechanics to implement. After your overview, rank project priorities: gameplay, polish, or art. This hierarchy helps you choose what to cut if time runs short. Misconception to avoid: the overview should not be a marketing blurb; it's a practical guide for design and technical choices. Close by writing your one-sentence elevator pitch — it will become the project's north star. GDD — High-level Overview & Elevator Pitch means an explicit elevator pitch and priorities list focus design decisions and prevent scope drift.. In practical terms, create a tight, informative start for your design document. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › GDD Overview
High-level overview

Start with title, genre, audience, and a concise elevator pitch that guides every decision.

Example pitch
"A bite-sized platformer where the player uses a charge-jump to navigate moving platforms and collect time shards across six short levels."
  • Write one sentence that defines the core experience.
  • List the top priority: gameplay, polish, or art—this sets trade-offs.
  • Keep the overview actionable, not promotional.
Priority matrix
Gameplay
Art
Polish
Choose one primary priority and one secondary to guide what to cut if time is tight.
Key Takeaway

An actionable one-sentence pitch directs design choices and prevents ambiguous goals.

screens.title: Core Gameplay: Mechanics & Core Loop
screens.narratorSegment: Core gameplay is the heart of your capstone. It defines the player's actions, feedback, and the loop they'll repeat while playing. A practical approach is to write mechanics as specific behaviors and numbers: movement speed, jump height, damage values, enemy patrol distances, and the exact sequence that constitutes the core loop. For example, a core loop might be: explore, collect item, return to hub, upgrade, repeat. Writing these steps prevents ambiguity during implementation and testing. A common misconception is that the core loop is naturally obvious; often it's not until you write it down that missing steps or friction points appear. Include clear win and loss conditions so testers know when the game ends and what success looks like. To ground this, imagine a top-down shooter where the loop is: spawn, defeat waves, collect power-up, progress to next arena; win by surviving three arenas. That clarity lets you scope enemies and level flow. Finish by listing three acceptance criteria for your MVP mechanic. Core Gameplay: Mechanics & Core Loop means write mechanics and the core loop with precise numbers and acceptance criteria to make implementation testable.. In practical terms, document precise mechanics, loops, and win/lose conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Core Gameplay
Mechanics: make them measurable
Document key numbers and behaviors so programmers and designers share the same expectations.
Sample mechanics
Player movement:
  - runSpeed = 6 units/s
  - jumpHeight = 2.5 units (calibrated with gravity)
Melee attack:
  - damage = 15
  - cooldown = 0.5s
Enemy patrol:
  - patrolPoints = [A,B]
  - detectionRadius = 3 units
Example core loop
Explore level → defeat enemies → collect power-up → return to hub → upgrade → repeat.
Acceptance criteria
  • Player can complete level start-to-finish without bugs that block progress.
  • Combat feels responsive: attack registers within expected frames and damage is consistent.
  • Enemies spawn and despawn without causing crashes or frame drops.
Common misconception
Assuming testers will infer mechanics. Always document explicit behavior and numbers to reduce assumptions.
Key Takeaway

Precise mechanics and core loops make the MVP implementable, testable, and polishable.

screens.title: Art, Audio & Mood: Making 'Feel' Specific
screens.narratorSegment: Art and audio define the player's immersion. Vague notes like "good graphics" or "epic music" are unhelpful; instead, pick a style reference, palette, and example tracks or mood words. For art, choose from pixel art, low-poly 3D, or stylized 2D and list constraints such as resolution, color palette, and asset counts. For audio, say whether music is looped or dynamic, list example moods, and note SFX priorities. A useful exercise is to collect two visual references and one audio reference and record why they fit the game's mood. A common mistake is over-scoping high-fidelity assets; for a capstone, favor consistent low-effort art that can be produced or sourced quickly. For instance, low-poly 3D with flat shading and a 3-color palette creates visual cohesion without long production time. The takeaway: be prescriptive about feel so art and audio work together to support gameplay rather than compete with it. What two references will you choose to define your game's mood? Art, Audio & Mood: Making 'Feel' Specific means choose explicit art and audio references to keep production focused and cohesive.. In practical terms, turn vague directions into concrete references and constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Art & Audio
Art direction
Specify style, palette, resolution, and asset limits so art remains achievable.
Example choices
Low-poly 3D, flat shading, 3-color palette, 200 collision-mesh-friendly assets max.
Quick rule
Pick one style and stick to its constraints to reduce iteration time.
Audio direction
Decide music style, whether it loops or reacts to gameplay, and the priority list of sound effects.
Example
Ambient synth loop for levels, distinct SFX for jump and hit, one short victory jingle.
Common mistake
Treating audio as optional. Even simple, consistent SFX greatly improve player feedback and polish.
Key Takeaway

Select clear references for art and audio, and define production-friendly constraints to ensure consistency and completion.

screens.title: Technical Specifications & Tools
screens.narratorSegment: The technical section of your GDD lists tools and constraints that affect implementation speed and feasibility. For this capstone, the engine is Unity and the language is C#. Specify target platforms like PC, WebGL, or mobile because each choice affects input handling, performance profiling, and asset requirements. Note any third-party tools you plan to use such as UI packages, audio middleware, or asset packs, and state licensing or integration notes. A common oversight is not considering performance budgets for target platforms: a mobile target will require lower-resolution textures and careful draw call management. Also add a short development environment note: your Unity version, preferred IDE, and branch/commit conventions for version control. This section is not exhaustive but should identify constraints that would force major design changes. The takeaway: early technical clarity reduces late surprises and informs realistic scope choices. Which platform constraints are most relevant to your game idea? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Technical Specs
Core technical choices
  • Engine: Unity
  • Language: C#
  • Target platforms: list priorities (e.g., PC, WebGL, mobile)
  • Key tools: UI package, audio tools, asset sources
Constraints and notes
Record Unity version, performance budgets, and any licensing requirements so future choices are informed.
Example note
Target WebGL: use compressed textures, limit draw calls, and test memory usage early.
Version control
Use Git even for solo projects. Specify branch naming, commit frequency, and asset storage strategy to avoid lost work.
Key Takeaway

Document constraints and tools early. Technical clarity prevents late rework and unrealistic scope.

screens.title: Minimal Viable Product (MVP) Planning
screens.narratorSegment: An MVP is the set of features that make your game playable, testable, and evaluable. For a capstone, it should be small enough to finish and polish within your timeline yet rich enough to convey the intended experience. Start by listing all candidate features, then prioritize: must-haves, nice-to-haves, and stretch goals. Choose 3–5 must-haves that cover the full player journey from start to finish. For example, for a platformer the must-haves might be player movement, one enemy type, level progression, collectibles, and a basic UI. A common error is including systems that only exist to support stretch goals; if a feature doesn't directly support the core experience, move it to stretch goals. Write clear acceptance criteria for each MVP feature so testers can confirm completion. The payoff is big: a well-scoped MVP reduces stress, increases polish, and gives you a reliable deliverable to iterate from. What are your three must-have features? In practical terms, define the smallest playable, testable version of your game. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › MVP Planning
MVP selection process
  1. List every feature you imagine.
  2. Mark as must-have, nice-to-have, or stretch goal.
  3. Keep only 3–5 must-haves that complete the core loop.
  4. Write acceptance criteria for each must-have.
Example: Platformer MVP
  • Player movement (run, jump) with acceptance test.
  • One enemy type with simple AI and damage.
  • Level progression and a scoring collectible.
Key Takeaway

An MVP protects your deadline and gives you a focused target to polish and test.

screens.title: Scope Creep — Causes & Mitigation
screens.narratorSegment: Scope creep happens when small, untracked additions shift a project beyond its intended scope. It often starts with well-meaning feature ideas, late inspiration, or pressure to add complexity. For a timed capstone this is dangerous: it leads to unfinished features, rushed polish, and stress. The best mitigation is discipline: define an MVP and a documented process for accepting changes. If a new idea appears, ask whether it is essential for the MVP or a stretch goal. If it is a stretch goal, record it and schedule it only after the MVP is complete. Another effective tactic is time-boxing: allocate short spikes for exploration and then decide whether to adopt the result. Use the GDD to log change requests and their impact on schedule and resources. Finally, keep weekly milestones and run short playtests to reveal whether new features actually improve the core experience. A small, well-finished game will always communicate your skills better than a large, unfinished one. How will you enforce your MVP boundaries? Scope Creep — Causes & Mitigation means document change requests and enforce mvp-first decisions to prevent uncontrolled project growth.. In practical terms, recognize how projects expand and keep your project on track. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Scope Creep
What causes scope creep?
  • Late ideas without cost estimates.
  • Vague requirements that invite specification growth.
  • Pressure to add features that don't serve the core loop.
Mitigation strategies
  • Define MVP and record stretch goals in the GDD.
  • Time-box experiments and require clear acceptance criteria.
  • Log change requests with impact estimates before approval.
Key Takeaway

Protect your MVP by making change requests explicit and evaluated against schedule impact.

screens.title: Version Control, Risk Assessment & Well-being
screens.narratorSegment: Protecting progress is both technical and personal. Version control, such as Git, is essential even for solo capstones: it records history, allows experimentation, and provides a safe rollback when something breaks. Describe your branching and commit conventions in the GDD so your workflow is consistent. Risk assessment is another short, high-value section: identify likely challenges such as complex AI, performance problems, or asset delays and list contingency plans. For example, if AI proves difficult, fall back to simpler patrol behavior as a backup. Also plan your schedule to prevent burnout: build small milestones, take regular breaks, and celebrate incremental wins. A common mistake is ignoring non-technical risks like scope and time pressure. Make a compact risk register with likelihood, impact, and an owner for each risk so you can respond quickly. The takeaway: combine version control and simple risk planning to keep momentum and safeguard your mental well-being while developing the capstone. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Version Control & Risk
Version control basics
Commit early and often. Use branches for features and keep a naming convention to make history readable.
Example convention
feature/short-description, fix/bug-id, chore/docs
Tip
Store large binary assets with LFS or a separate asset repository to keep Git responsive.
Risk register
List risks, likelihood, impact, owner, and contingency. Update this during major milestones.
Example entry
Risk: Complex AI. Likelihood: Medium. Impact: High. Contingency: Use simple patrol AI and increase level design variety.
Well-being
Set realistic goals, schedule breaks, and celebrate small milestones to avoid burnout.
Key Takeaway

Combine version control with a simple risk plan to protect your work and your schedule.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › GDD Outline
Draft Your Capstone GDD Outline

Use this template as a practical starting point. Keep entries short and testable.

# My Capstone Game Design Document

## 1. Game Overview
### 1.1 Title: [Your Game Title Here]
### 1.2 Genre: [e.g., 2D Platformer, Top-Down Shooter, Puzzle]
### 1.3 Elevator Pitch: [1-2 sentences describing your game's core appeal]

## 2. Core Gameplay
### 2.1 Player Character & Controls:
  - [Describe player abilities, movement, and input scheme with numbers]
### 2.2 Core Loop:
  - [What does the player do repeatedly? e.g., "Collect coins, avoid enemies, reach exit."]
### 2.3 Win/Loss Conditions:
  - [How does the player win? How do they lose?]
### 2.4 Key Mechanics (MVP):
  - [3-5 essential features with acceptance criteria]

## 3. World & Narrative
### 3.1 Setting/Theme:
  - [Describe the game's world and overall atmosphere]
### 3.2 Story (if any):
  - [Brief plot summary or background lore]

## 4. Art & Audio
### 4.1 Visual Style:
  - [e.g., Pixel art, low-poly 3D, cartoonish]
### 4.2 UI/UX Style:
  - [How will the user interface look and feel?]
### 4.3 Audio Direction:
  - [Music and SFX approach]

## 5. Technical Specifications
### 5.1 Engine: Unity
### 5.2 Programming Language: C#
### 5.3 Target Platform(s): [e.g., PC Standalone, WebGL]
### 5.4 Key Assets/Tools:
  - [List any specific assets or tools you plan to use]

## 6. Risk Register
- Risk: [describe], Impact: [High/Medium/Low], Contingency: [plan]
When your draft is ready, commit it to version control to celebrate the first checkpoint.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Quick Reference
Minimal Viable Product
Keep 3–5 must-have features that complete the player journey and are testable.
Version Control

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to the capstone kickoff. This project is your chance to integrate Unity, C#, and design skills into a single, polished game you can show to employers or peers. The aim is not to build a blockbuster but to produce a complete, well-scoped playable experience that demonstrates your strengths. In this lesson you will learn why planning matters, how a Game Design Document acts as a single source of truth, and how to protect your schedule by defining a minimal viable product. I'll guide you through each GDD section — concept, core gameplay, art and audio, technical specs — and show practical ways to keep scope under control. You'll also get simple risk-management practices such as version control and realistic milestone planning. By the end you'll know what to write in your first GDD draft and how to use it every week to steer development. Think of this kickoff as building the map before you walk the terrain: the map doesn't limit creativity, it helps you finish. What is one small but essential feature your capstone must include?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the purpose of a capstone project, start a game with a clear vision, and write the first draft of a Game Design Document. You will learn to identify the GDD sections that matter most: high-level overview, core gameplay, art and audio direction, technical specifications, and a risk plan. You will also practice defining a minimal viable product, which protects your schedule and ensures a playable deliverable. Each objective includes a practical reason: employers and collaborators want demonstrable results, and a structured plan helps you prioritize work and make defensible trade-offs. We'll show examples of concrete MVP features and common vague statements to avoid. Finally, you'll be introduced to simple project-safety practices such as version control, realistic milestones, and short feedback loops to reduce burnout. These skills let you go from idea to a finished, playable capstone with confidence. Which objective do you want to start with first?

These objectives are practical. Understanding the GDD and MVP means you can scope tasks into weekly milestones, defend feature trade-offs, and give reviewers a clear playable build. Learning version control prepares you to recover from mistakes and collaborate without fear. Recognizing common pitfalls like vague specifications or scope creep helps you avoid them before they derail development. Each learning goal maps to a real activity: write the GDD first draft, implement the MVP, make a Git commit every day, and log risks with contingency plans. We'll also practice articulating three core features that must exist for your game to be testable. This habit of precise specification speeds design iteration and reduces rework. As you prepare your capstone, these skills let you move from an idea to a reproducible project timeline, and they make your final submission credible. Which habit will you adopt first?

A capstone project is a culminating piece of work that gathers your skills into a single, demonstrable product. In game development, it's an opportunity to show you can design, implement, and polish a playable experience in Unity using C#. It matters because hiring teams and reviewers look for finished artifacts that reveal both creative design choices and technical competence. A common misconception is that bigger equals better. In reality, a focused, complete game that demonstrates thoughtful systems and polish beats an incomplete, sprawling concept. For example, a tight 2D platformer with a solid core loop, responsive controls, and a handful of levels will communicate more than an unfinished ambitious RPG. When planning, state your goals: is the capstone about showcasing gameplay, technical systems, or art direction? Choose one primary focus. Your takeaway is this: pick a realistic scope that highlights your strengths and commit to finishing the playable MVP. Which single skill do you want this capstone to showcase? What is a Capstone Project? means a capstone demonstrates mastery through a finished, playable game that highlights your strongest skills.. In practical terms, define the capstone and its role in your learning journey. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Game Design Document is your project's compass. It collects the elevator pitch, target audience, mechanics, art and audio directions, and technical notes into one place so design decisions remain consistent over time. A common error is to treat the GDD as a static checklist. Instead, view it as living: update it after playtests, record why features changed, and use it to communicate with collaborators or future-you. Practically, start the GDD with a one-paragraph overview and a clear MVP list. Then expand the core gameplay section with concrete numbers: movement speeds, jump heights, enemy behavior patterns, and win/loss conditions. Being specific eliminates ambiguous goals like "fun combat." For example, note that an enemy patrols between two points, deals two damage per hit, and has a 0.5-second stagger when hit. That detail guides programming and tuning. The takeaway: a GDD reduces wasted effort and helps you finish by making decisions explicit. What would you write in your GDD's one-sentence elevator pitch? Why a Game Design Document (GDD)? means a living gdd records decisions and guides consistent development, avoiding ambiguity and rework.. In practical terms, use a gdd as a living blueprint and single source of truth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Begin your GDD with a high-level overview that answers the core questions: what is the game, who is it for, and what makes it compelling? This includes a working title, genre, target audience, and a one- or two-sentence elevator pitch. Why is this important? Because a clear overview aligns every later decision with the game's primary goals. A vague pitch invites scope drift. For example, compare "a platformer with good combat" to "a bite-sized platformer where the player uses a charge-jump to navigate moving platforms and collect time shards across six short levels." The second version immediately suggests level design constraints and mechanics to implement. After your overview, rank project priorities: gameplay, polish, or art. This hierarchy helps you choose what to cut if time runs short. Misconception to avoid: the overview should not be a marketing blurb; it's a practical guide for design and technical choices. Close by writing your one-sentence elevator pitch — it will become the project's north star. GDD — High-level Overview & Elevator Pitch means an explicit elevator pitch and priorities list focus design decisions and prevent scope drift.. In practical terms, create a tight, informative start for your design document. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core gameplay is the heart of your capstone. It defines the player's actions, feedback, and the loop they'll repeat while playing. A practical approach is to write mechanics as specific behaviors and numbers: movement speed, jump height, damage values, enemy patrol distances, and the exact sequence that constitutes the core loop. For example, a core loop might be: explore, collect item, return to hub, upgrade, repeat. Writing these steps prevents ambiguity during implementation and testing. A common misconception is that the core loop is naturally obvious; often it's not until you write it down that missing steps or friction points appear. Include clear win and loss conditions so testers know when the game ends and what success looks like. To ground this, imagine a top-down shooter where the loop is: spawn, defeat waves, collect power-up, progress to next arena; win by surviving three arenas. That clarity lets you scope enemies and level flow. Finish by listing three acceptance criteria for your MVP mechanic. Core Gameplay: Mechanics & Core Loop means write mechanics and the core loop with precise numbers and acceptance criteria to make implementation testable.. In practical terms, document precise mechanics, loops, and win/lose conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Art and audio define the player's immersion. Vague notes like "good graphics" or "epic music" are unhelpful; instead, pick a style reference, palette, and example tracks or mood words. For art, choose from pixel art, low-poly 3D, or stylized 2D and list constraints such as resolution, color palette, and asset counts. For audio, say whether music is looped or dynamic, list example moods, and note SFX priorities. A useful exercise is to collect two visual references and one audio reference and record why they fit the game's mood. A common mistake is over-scoping high-fidelity assets; for a capstone, favor consistent low-effort art that can be produced or sourced quickly. For instance, low-poly 3D with flat shading and a 3-color palette creates visual cohesion without long production time. The takeaway: be prescriptive about feel so art and audio work together to support gameplay rather than compete with it. What two references will you choose to define your game's mood? Art, Audio & Mood: Making 'Feel' Specific means choose explicit art and audio references to keep production focused and cohesive.. In practical terms, turn vague directions into concrete references and constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The technical section of your GDD lists tools and constraints that affect implementation speed and feasibility. For this capstone, the engine is Unity and the language is C#. Specify target platforms like PC, WebGL, or mobile because each choice affects input handling, performance profiling, and asset requirements. Note any third-party tools you plan to use such as UI packages, audio middleware, or asset packs, and state licensing or integration notes. A common oversight is not considering performance budgets for target platforms: a mobile target will require lower-resolution textures and careful draw call management. Also add a short development environment note: your Unity version, preferred IDE, and branch/commit conventions for version control. This section is not exhaustive but should identify constraints that would force major design changes. The takeaway: early technical clarity reduces late surprises and informs realistic scope choices. Which platform constraints are most relevant to your game idea? Technical Specifications & Tools means define engine, language, platforms, and essential tools so technical limits shape design from the start.. In practical terms, decide engine, language, platforms, and key tools up front. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An MVP is the set of features that make your game playable, testable, and evaluable. For a capstone, it should be small enough to finish and polish within your timeline yet rich enough to convey the intended experience. Start by listing all candidate features, then prioritize: must-haves, nice-to-haves, and stretch goals. Choose 3–5 must-haves that cover the full player journey from start to finish. For example, for a platformer the must-haves might be player movement, one enemy type, level progression, collectibles, and a basic UI. A common error is including systems that only exist to support stretch goals; if a feature doesn't directly support the core experience, move it to stretch goals. Write clear acceptance criteria for each MVP feature so testers can confirm completion. The payoff is big: a well-scoped MVP reduces stress, increases polish, and gives you a reliable deliverable to iterate from. What are your three must-have features? Scope creep happens when small, untracked additions shift a project beyond its intended scope. It often starts with well-meaning feature ideas, late inspiration, or pressure to add complexity. For a timed capstone this is dangerous: it leads to unfinished features, rushed polish, and stress. The best mitigation is discipline: define an MVP and a documented process for accepting changes. If a new idea appears, ask whether it is essential for the MVP or a stretch goal. If it is a stretch goal, record it and schedule it only after the MVP is complete. Another effective tactic is time-boxing: allocate short spikes for exploration and then decide whether to adopt the result. Use the GDD to log change requests and their impact on schedule and resources. Finally, keep weekly milestones and run short playtests to reveal whether new features actually improve the core experience. A small, well-finished game will always communicate your skills better than a large, unfinished one. How will you enforce your MVP boundaries?
